gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a heart-rate error figure for its picks against a reference sensor. OutdoorGearLab measured a 1.0 bpm median difference for the Garmin vívoactive 6 and ±3 bpm for the Fitbit Charge 6. Expert Reviews measured a 0.91% average difference for the Apple Watch Series 11. TechGearLab scored the WHOOP 5.0 lowest of the four at 94.44%.
standout_why: I compared against the two cited pages and the top uncited result. WIRED (published 2026-06-19, updated August 2026) has no heart-rate, GPS or battery measurements: its battery figures are maker specs, and on the Charge 6 it says only that heart rate 'held up well', with no number. Men's Health has no chest-strap comparison. Its only accuracy remark is Ebenezer Samuel saying WHOOP 'is almost always overshooting' on heart rate, so the WHOOP doubt is there but has no number. Android Authority (2026-01-22) has only qualitative heart-rate notes and its author's battery estimates. None of the three puts measured figures for the vívoactive 6, Charge 6, Series 11 and WHOOP 5.0 side by side. I could not load Tom's Guide's list, and I did not open TechRadar, NBC Select, Engadget, Strategist or Men's Journal. WIRED and Men's Health were blocked to direct fetch, so I read them through the r.jina.ai reader. The Men's Health page it returned showed a 2024-03-15 publish date and a pick list (WHOOP 5.0, Oura, Instinct 3 and others) that differs from the June 2026 listing ChatGPT got. It may be a different version of the page.
decides: The finding backs ChatGPT's order for gym and running use. The vívoactive 6 (1.0 bpm median against an armband, ±0.04 mi over 2 miles, 20 h GPS measured) and the Series 11 (0.91% against a chest belt) are the accurate picks. The Charge 6 is good enough on heart rate (±3 bpm against a Polar H10) but its GPS is weak: it was 0.86 mi off on a steep hill and lasted about 8 h of GPS. ChatGPT called the WHOOP 5.0 'best for serious training', but it had the lowest heart-rate score of the four (94.44%, TechGearLab). the5krunner found wrist-worn WHOOP heart rate wrong in hard efforts, and DC Rainmaker counted 530 steps on a 500-step walk. Men who lift or do intervals should be told to wear it on the bicep or pair a chest strap. Our page's Helio Strap row gains a direct comparison: it counted 505 on the same 500-step test.

findings.note: The reference was a chest strap, covering resting, activity-average and max heart rate. TechGearLab does not say how the percentage is calculated. The comparison scores come from TechGearLab's best-fitness-tracker table, which covers the vívoactive 5 and Watch 10, not the vívoactive 6 or Series 11.

unsourced: Tom's Guide's Apple Watch Series 11 battery test (drain figures): WebFetch got the header only with no article body, and the r.jina.ai reader returned HTTP 403. The figures appeared only in search snippets, so they are left out.

A WSJ (Nicole Nguyen) test comparing the Series 11 with WHOOP, Oura and Fitbit, reported as ±2 bpm: I found it only on the aggregator news.lavx.hu and did not open the WSJ original, so it is left out.

A bpm or percentage wrist heart-rate error for the WHOOP 5.0 against a chest strap with a stated method: TechGearLab gives a percentage without a formula, and the5krunner and DC Rainmaker publish charts only.
A measured WHOOP 5.0 battery life from a named tester: TechGearLab and DC Rainmaker's Cirqa article give only the claim or no figure, and I did not open DC Rainmaker's 2025 backlog post.
A measured vívoactive 6 heart-rate error against a chest strap (not an armband): the only numeric figure I opened uses a Polar Verity Sense.
TechRadar's, NBC Select's and Engadget's lists: not opened, so I can't rule out that they carry measured figures.
